extracted.intended_audience: experimental natural philosophers / physicists studying fluid resistance and hydrodynamic experiments (17th-century style)
extracted.subtask_description: Determine and characterize the resistance experienced by spherical bodies moving in various fluids, using theoretical reasoning and pendulum-based experiments to deduce scaling with velocity, size, and fluid properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efflux velocity relation (Torricelli-style statement)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Est igitur velocitas quacum aqua exit e foramine, ad velocitatem quam aqua cadens, & tempore T cadendo describens spatium S acquireret, ut altitudo aquæ foramini perpendiculariter incumbentis, ad medium proportionale inter altitudinem illam duplicatam & spatium illud S, quod corpus tempore T cadendo describeret."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Velocity of efflux from an orifice is related to the velocity a falling body would acquire in the same time; specifically it is proportional to a mean proportional between twice the head above the orifice and the free-fall distance S. Applicable under the assumption of a "fluidum subtilissimum" (very fluid medium). Caveat: thicker fluids or narrow orifices cause slower efflux than this ideal relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trajectory of oblique efflux (parabolic path)
rubrics_metrics.description: "si egrediatur oblique per canalem in latus vasis, describet in spatiis non resistentibus Parabolam cujus latus rectum est altitudo aquæ in vase supra canalis orificium..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a jet issues obliquely into nonresisting space, its path is a parabola whose latus rectum equals the height of the water above the orifice; axis perpendicular to horizon through the orifice. Use this for predicting jet shapes when neglecting air resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hydrostatic pressure removal by an aperture
rubrics_metrics.description: "vas sustinebit pondus aquæ totius, non obstante effluxu, sed latus vasis de quo effluit non sustinebit pressionem illam omnem. Tolletur enim pressio partis illius ubi perforatur: quæ quidem pressio æqualis est ponderi columnæ aquæ, cujus basis foramini æquatur & altitudo eadem est quæ aquæ totius supra foramen."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opening a horizontal outlet removes the pressure on the part of the vessel where perforated equal to the weight of the column of water with base equal to the orifice and height equal to the water above it. This affects net forces on vessel walls and must be accounted for in experiments and thought experiments (e.g., suspended vessel will tilt/recede accordingly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Action–reaction between globe and flowing fluid (force equivalence)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Actio & reactio aquæ per motus Legem tertiam æquantur inter se... actio contraria aquæ in Globum æqualis est vi quæ motum eundem vel tollere vel generare possit, hoc est ponderi columnæ aquæ, quæ Globo perpendiculariter imminet & cujus altitudo est RS."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The force exerted by flowing fluid on a body equals the counterforce the body exerts on the fluid; can be treated as equal to the weight of a column of fluid whose base equals the body's cross-section and whose height is the local fluid head (RS). Use this to relate measured momentum-change of effluent to force on the immersed body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of blocked flow to cross-sectional areas (globe in a channel)
rubrics_metrics.description: "quantitas aquæ ... est ut quadratum diametri Globi ad quadratum diametri cavitatis canalis."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The quantity of fluid whose descent a globe prevents (in a channel) is proportional to the square of the globe's diameter relative to the square of the channel cavity's diameter (i.e., proportional to the area of the annular passage). Use this geometric ratio to compute the effective flow area when a sphere nearly fills a channel; applicable when fluid is 'fluidissimum'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma IV — entrainment principle (homogeneous fluid carried with vessel)
rubrics_metrics.description: "partes Fluidi inclusi, æqualiter participando motum vasis, quiescent inter se... Fluidum omne quod motu progressivo accelerato fertur, & cujus partes inter se quiescunt, solida quæcunque ejusdem densitatis inclusa... rapit secum."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a vessel with homogeneous fluid is accelerated so that fluid parts have no relative motion, the fluid moves uniformly and will carry along any solids of the same density. This supports reasoning about entrainment and when a fluid will drag along inclusions rather than slip past them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asymptotic/scaling behavior as solid size increases (Prop. XL)
rubrics_metrics.description: "In Fluido quocunque dato inveniatur resistentia ultima solidi specie dati, cujus magnitudo in infinitum augetur... resistentia solidi aucti... dabitur per proportionem superiorem... ut spatium Cylindricum per quod solidum movetur, adeoque in duplicata ratione semidiametri solidi quamproxime."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a solid's size grows without bound in a given fluid, its resistance approaches a limiting scaling determined by the quantity of fluid displaced (roughly a cylindrical volume): resistance scales approximately with the square of the semidiameter (i.e., cross-sectional area). Hence subdividing the fluid into ever smaller 'particles' will not indefinitely reduce resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decomposition of resistance into velocity-dependent terms (A, B, C model)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Designet jam V velocitatem maximam ... fingamus quod differentia arcuum sit AV + BV^{3/2} + CV^2..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirically express resistance-related arc-differences as a polynomial (or mixed-power) function of velocity: AV + B V^{3/2} + C V^2. Determine coefficients A,B,C from multiple pendulum observations at different amplitudes/velocities by solving the resulting linear system. Note: in many experiments the V^2 term dominates at higher velocities; A (linear) and B (V^{3/2}) capture low-velocity/viscous contributions or transitional behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental method using pendulum decay to quantify resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure initial descent arc and final ascent arc after motion loss; count oscillations until specified fraction of motion is lost; convert arcs to velocities (via chord/arc relations and cycloid corrections); use these data to compute resistive coefficients and total resistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple amplitudes (different initial arcs) to generate independent equations; correct for the geometric relation between chord/arc and velocity (circle vs cycloid subtleties); transform observed arc-differences and oscillation counts into proportional resistances. Tables of arc-descents, ascents, and oscillation counts are given as examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental controls and corrections to ensure valid resistance measurements
rubrics_metrics.description: Notes and experiments emphasise: subtract the filament's resistance; ensure globes are accurately spherical; use sufficiently wide vases/canals to avoid boundary effects; if the filament is immersed or vessel is narrow the measured resistance is substantially affected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure and remove contribution of suspension filament (can be a large fraction). Ensure vessel dimensions are large relative to sphere diameter to avoid confinement effects. Prefer larger spheres in geometric progression and larger vessels for more reliable asymptotic behavior. Beware of imperfect sphericity and experimental imprecision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence of resistance on fluid density and fluid type
rubrics_metrics.description: "resistentia argenti vivi ad resistentiam aquæ ut 13 vel 14 ad 1 circiter: id est ut densitas argenti vivi ad densitatem aquæ..." and general statements that resistances of fast-moving bodies are approximately proportional to fluid density.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical experiments indicate resistance scales approximately like the density of the fluid (e.g., mercury ~13–14× water). Use density ratios to compare resistances across fluids, while noting viscosity and other fluid properties may modify exact proportions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of viscosity / 'crassities' of fluid particles
rubrics_metrics.description: "Nam si aqua ex partibus crassioribus constet, hæc tardius effluet..." and later: "Nam Fluida tenaciora pari densitate proculdubio magis resistunt..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the fluid consists of coarser/thicker particles (higher viscosity or cohesive behavior), efflux and transits are slower and resistance is higher than predictions for an ideal 'fluidum subtilissimum'. Temperature, fluid composition, and cohesion (e.g., oils vs water) change resistance; experimental rules must be applied only to sufficiently fluid media or corrected for viscosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Velocity-regime distinctions: slow vs fast motion scaling
rubrics_metrics.description: Corollaries and scholium: for faster motion resistance in anterior surface is approximately in duplicate ratio of velocities (i.e., ~V^2), but for slower motion resistance is somewhat larger than the duplicate ratio; experiments show transitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret measured data with attention to velocity regime: at higher speeds the quadratic (V^2) term dominates and scaling with area and fluid density applies; at lower speeds additional (linear or fractional-power) terms become significant, producing deviations from pure quadratic scaling.

rubrics_metrics.name: High-speed/wake effect increasing resistance beyond simple quadratic law
rubrics_metrics.description: "Nam corpora longe velocissima spatium a tergo relinquent vacuum, ideoque resistentia ... nullatenus minuetur per pressionem Medii in partibus posticis... resistentia tandem evadet quasi triplo major quam pro Regula generali novissime posita."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At very high speeds a body may leave a near-vacuum behind it so the rear cannot refill fast enough; this increases resistance beyond the simple quadratic rule, potentially up to ~3× the general quadratic estimate in extreme cases. Recognize this when extrapolating from moderate-speed experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric and kinematic corrections (cycloid vs circle, chord–arc relations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of converting observed arc lengths and chord relations: "cum velocitates maximæ sint in Cycloide ut arcus oscillando descripti, in circulo vero ut semissium arcuum illorum chordæ... tempora autem in circulo sint majora quam in Cycloide in velocitatis ratione reciproca" and resulting correction factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convert oscillation arc measurements to velocities accounting for the pendulum path geometry (cycloidal vs circular approximation). Use derived correction factors when comparing theory predictions to observed arc amplitudes and timing; failure to correct yields systematic error in inferred resistances.
